analysis.one_liner: Requires new large trucks and trailers to carry side guards that stop cars and people from sliding underneath in crashes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 9 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has taken no action and held no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Transportation Department to write rules forcing side underride guards onto all new large trucks, trailers, and single-unit trucks within about 18 months of enactment, with full compliance two years later. These guards keep a car that hits the side of a truck from sliding underneath it, and keep motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians from being run under as well. The bill also revives a federal advisory committee on underride crashes, publishes government research on a public website, and orders studies on front-override crashes and rear-guard enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who drives or rides near large trucks: passenger car occupants whose cars can currently slide under the side of a trailer in a side-impact crash, and motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians who can be run under along a trailer's side. The bill's own findings cite an advisory committee report counting roughly 25,100 underride crashes and 31,500 deaths over the more than 50 years since NHTSA was created, with no substantial federal progress, and note the National Transportation Safety Board has recommended front, rear, and side guards on tractor-trailers and rear and side guards on single-unit trucks [S2]. Victim families also gain a formal seat: the bill expands the Advisory Committee on Underride Protection to include families of underride crash victims and requires it to meet monthly until final rules are issued [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car occupants, motorcyclists, bicyclists, and pedestrians

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Secretary to finalize, within 18 months of enactment, safety standards mandating side underride guards on new trailers, semitrailers, and single-unit trucks, with full compliance no later than 2 years after the rules are finalized.

Sets a concrete performance bar: side guards must prevent intrusion into a passenger car's occupant survival space in a perpendicular crash at speeds up to 40 mph, and must impede vulnerable road users from sliding under the side of a truck. The guards must also be integrated with aerodynamic design so they do not worsen fuel economy.

Reconvenes the Advisory Committee on Underride Protection within 180 days, expands its membership to include families of underride crash victims, and requires monthly meetings until final regulations are issued, then at least annual meetings.

Creates a public website publishing all federal underride research, rulemaking information, victim stories, and crash data, updated at least quarterly, so researchers, advocates, and the public can see what the government knows.
Orders a National Academies study on front-of-truck underride (override) crashes and a GAO study on how well NHTSA's 2022 rear-impact-guard rule is actually being implemented.

Directs NHTSA to review federal crash data to count how many underride deaths go unreported by state and local police, and to build free web training so officers identify underride crashes correctly in the future.

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and the manufacturers of trailers, semitrailers, and single-unit trucks, who must equip every new vehicle with side underride guards that meet the performance standard. Those equipment costs would be passed into freight prices. The public also pays indirectly for the advisory committee, studies, and website, though these are modest administrative costs.

drawbacks.text: Every new trailer, semitrailer, and single-unit truck must carry side underride guards, adding real equipment cost to fleets; the bill recognizes the weight-and-efficiency tradeoff by requiring guards to be integrated with fuel-saving aerodynamic design and by making regulators count net fuel savings in the cost-benefit analysis, but it does not cap compliance costs, and carriers would likely pass them into shipping prices.

The protections arrive slowly: rules are due 18 months after enactment and full compliance is not required until 2 years after that, meaning new guards reach the road gradually and only on newly built trucks and trailers, not the existing fleet.

The bill mandates side guards but only commissions studies on front-override protection and on enforcing the existing rear-guard rule, so deaths at the front of large trucks and weaknesses in rear-guard enforcement remain unresolved even if it passes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: side guards convert side-impact truck crashes that today slide a car under a trailer, where occupant protection fails, into survivable crashes, and they stop people on foot, bikes, and motorcycles from being run under. The cost is equipment on new trucks and trailers, borne by fleets and passed into freight prices, partially offset by required aerodynamic fuel savings. The strongest honest objection is timing and scope: the fleet turns over slowly, front-override deaths are only studied rather than addressed, and the cost-benefit arithmetic for side guards has been contested. On balance this is a targeted, incremental safety mandate whose benefits accrue to the public and whose costs are real but modest per vehicle.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the Stop Underrides Act 2.0 on February 4, 2026, joined by five original cosponsors, and named the bill in memory of dozens of named underride crash victims.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, its only committee assignment.
Nine senators in total, all Democrats, have signed on as cosponsors; no Republican has joined.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred, and the bill has sat in committee since referral; Congress remains in session through early January 2027.

The bill is written to force action the administration has been backing away from: it includes a clause ensuring that even if the Transportation Secretary withdraws NHTSA's 2023 advance notice of proposed rulemaking on side underride guards, the Secretary must still finalize the mandated regulations.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nobody has had to act: trailer and single-unit truck manufacturers and carriers avoid any new equipment mandate as long as the bill sits untouched in the Commerce Committee, and the current weak federal approach to side underride rulemaking continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Trailer and truck makers, for now

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote it to mandate side underride guard rules, revive the underride advisory committee, and require studies and public reporting.

for.name: Sens. Lujan, Blumenthal, Van Hollen, Duckworth, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined Gillibrand as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Four additional Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Brought the cosponsor total to 9, all Democrats.

for.name: Families of underride crash victims and underride safety advocates
for.what_they_did: Pushed for comprehensive underride protection; the bill memorializes dozens of named victims and adds victim families to the federal advisory committee, and its findings quote the advisory committee's report that no substantial progress has been made on underride prevention.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill since it was referred in February 2026: no hearing or markup, leaving it without a path to the floor.

against.name: Trucking and trailer manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: Has historically opposed mandatory side underride guards on cost and weight grounds; the bill itself anticipates resistance by counting net fuel savings in the cost-benefit analysis and by guarding against withdrawal of NHTSA's side underride rulemaking.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors plus the sponsor are Democrats and no Republican has signed on, but no floor vote has occurred, so the actual partisan split has never been tested.

industries.note: The bill requires every new trailer and semitrailer to carry side underride guards meeting a 40-mph crash-performance standard within roughly 3.5 years of enactment, a direct redesign-and-equip mandate. Their cost of compliance is the public's safety gain, which is why their interest in this bill runs against ordinary road users.

Fleets buy the newly guarded trailers and single-unit trucks, absorbing higher equipment prices that would flow into freight costs. In exchange their vehicles become less lethal to car occupants and vulnerable road users in side-impact crashes.
The mandate extends beyond tractor-trailers to single-unit trucks, requiring rear and side underride protection on a vehicle class that current rules cover less completely.

The performance standard requires guards to be integrated with fuel-saving aerodynamics, and the cost-benefit analysis counts fuel savings, favoring combination side-skirt/guard products and expanding their market to every new trailer and truck.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to Senate Commerce rarely reach the floor on their own, and this one has no Republican cosponsors, so as a standalone bill it is likely to sit in committee. Its more realistic path is having its underride provisions folded into the next surface transportation reauthorization bill, where similar safety mandates have historically traveled.
